title: Langfuse And LangChain Flashcard Feed
summary: Passive AI engineering cards for reviewing LLM application architecture, LangChain, LangGraph, Langfuse tracing, RAG quality, evaluations, and risk governance.
audience: Engineers learning to build, operate, evaluate, and govern production LLM applications.

cards.title: AI Product Loop
cards.prompt: A production LLM feature is a loop: build, trace, evaluate, and improve.
cards.explanation: The model call is only one part of the system. The product becomes reliable when prompt versions, retrieval, tools, traces, datasets, scores, and release decisions reinforce each other.

cards.title: Model As Dependency
cards.prompt: Treat the model as a probabilistic dependency, not as product logic by itself.
cards.explanation: The application still owns timeouts, retries, validation, output policy, fallbacks, tracing, and user-visible behavior even when a model creates the text.

cards.title: Trust Buckets
cards.prompt: Separate user-controlled, system-controlled, and model-generated data.
cards.explanation: Trust buckets prevent model output or retrieved text from being treated as authority. They make validation and safety review much easier to reason about.

cards.title: Trace Early
cards.prompt: Add tracing before the first serious prompt iteration, not after production confusion.
cards.explanation: Without traces, teams argue from anecdotes. With traces, they can inspect prompt versions, context, tool calls, token usage, latency, errors, and evaluation outcomes.

cards.title: Fallback Is Behavior
cards.prompt: Design the fallback path as a product behavior, not an exception nobody sees.
cards.explanation: A clear fallback protects users when retrieval fails, tool calls error, confidence is low, or policy cannot be satisfied. It should be traced and evaluated.

cards.title: Cost Needs Context
cards.prompt: Debug model spend by feature, prompt version, model, token count, and user job.
cards.explanation: Aggregate cost alone rarely explains what changed. Feature and prompt metadata show whether the cost came from longer context, verbose outputs, retries, or model choice.

cards.title: Request Summary Snippet
cards.prompt: A compact request summary can power review dashboards and incident notes.
cards.explanation: Keep summaries structured and safe. They should expose review facts without copying unnecessary prompt or user content into logs.
cards.code:
const totalTokens = event.inputTokens + event.outputTokens;
const usedRetrieval = event.retrievedSourceIds.length > 0;

cards.title: Status Label Snippet
cards.prompt: Turn status and token usage into an explicit review label.
cards.explanation: Small deterministic helpers make production review repeatable. They are easier to test than logic hidden in prompt text.

cards.title: Safe Metadata Snippet
cards.prompt: Record ids and counts before copying raw content into telemetry.
cards.explanation: Source ids, prompt version, route, status, and counts often answer debugging questions without storing sensitive source material.

cards.title: Explain The Loop
cards.prompt: How would you explain the LLM application improvement loop to a backend engineer?
cards.explanation: A strong answer says the loop starts with user job definition, records traces, builds datasets from real cases, scores outputs, and promotes changes with evidence.

cards.title: Prototype To Production
cards.prompt: What changes when an LLM prototype becomes a production feature?
cards.explanation: Production adds ownership of validation, privacy, cost, latency, fallbacks, evaluation, trace access, prompt change control, and incident response.

cards.title: Trust Boundary Review
cards.prompt: Why should model-generated tool arguments be validated outside the model?
cards.explanation: The model can propose data, but the application owns permissions, schemas, idempotency, and safety checks before any deterministic action runs.

cards.title: Tool Contract
cards.prompt: A LangChain tool should be narrow, named clearly, and backed by an input schema.
cards.explanation: A useful tool is not just a function. It is an application boundary where model intent becomes validated deterministic work.

cards.title: Structured Output
cards.prompt: Use structured output when downstream code needs fields instead of prose.
cards.explanation: Structured output helps extraction, routing, and automation, but the application still validates whether the returned shape is acceptable for the next step.

cards.title: RAG Is Context
cards.prompt: RAG retrieves trusted context and asks the model to answer from it.
cards.explanation: The model should not be expected to know product-specific or current facts from training. Retrieval supplies source material at request time.

cards.title: Start Small
cards.prompt: Use a simple chain before an agent when the steps are already known.
cards.explanation: A deterministic flow is easier to debug, test, trace, and secure. Add agent flexibility only when product behavior needs dynamic choice.

cards.title: Tool Permission
cards.prompt: Do not let a model bypass authorization just because it selected a tool.
cards.explanation: Tool calls cross from language generation into application action. Authorization, validation, and rate limits must stay outside the prompt.

cards.title: RAG Fallback
cards.prompt: A missing source should produce a clear fallback, not a confident guess.
cards.explanation: A RAG system is safer when it admits missing context. The fallback should be traced so teams can improve retrieval or source coverage.

cards.title: Tool Schema Snippet
cards.prompt: Tool schemas make model-selected actions reviewable and testable.
cards.explanation: The schema documents what the tool accepts and gives the application a validation point before any side effect happens.

cards.title: Router Snippet
cards.prompt: Low-confidence model classifications should not drive tool execution.
cards.explanation: Confidence thresholds are product policy. Keep them visible in code so they can be tested and reviewed.
cards.code: if (confidence < 0.75) return { needsHumanApproval: true, reason: 'low confidence' };

cards.title: RAG Source Snippet
cards.prompt: Pass source ids through the flow so answers can be reviewed later.
cards.explanation: Source ids connect retrieval, prompt context, citations, and evaluation. Without them, bad answers are harder to diagnose.

cards.title: Chain Or Agent
cards.prompt: How do you decide whether to use a simple chain or an agent?
cards.explanation: A strong answer starts with deterministic workflows for known steps and uses agents only when dynamic tool or step selection is necessary.

cards.title: Tool Review
cards.prompt: What makes a LangChain tool safe enough for production?
cards.explanation: Safe tools are narrow, schema-validated, authorized, rate-limited, least-privilege, traced, and explicit about side effects.

cards.title: RAG Explanation
cards.prompt: Explain RAG to someone who thinks the model should already know the answer.
cards.explanation: RAG gives the model current trusted context at request time. It is useful for private, changing, or source-bound knowledge.

cards.title: Trace Timeline
cards.prompt: A trace is one request or task timeline across the LLM application.
cards.explanation: The trace lets engineers inspect prompt assembly, retrieval, tools, generation, output checks, errors, latency, tokens, and status in one place.

cards.title: Generation Observation
cards.prompt: A generation records model-specific behavior inside a trace.
cards.explanation: Generation observations are where prompt, response, model name, token usage, latency, and model errors become debuggable.

cards.title: Session Grouping
cards.prompt: A session groups related traces across a multi-turn user journey.
cards.explanation: Sessions help teams review a conversation or workflow that spans several requests while keeping each trace focused on one request or task.

cards.title: Safe Trace Metadata
cards.prompt: Prefer stable ids, counts, and labels over raw sensitive content in metadata.
cards.explanation: Good metadata makes traces searchable while reducing privacy risk. It should be designed intentionally rather than copied from request bodies.

cards.title: Cost Debugging
cards.prompt: Cost spikes need prompt version, model, context size, retries, and feature labels.
cards.explanation: Token counts alone do not tell the story. Teams need trace metadata that explains which release or product behavior changed.

cards.title: Stable Trace Shape
cards.prompt: A stable trace shape makes incidents easier to compare across requests.
cards.explanation: When every request has the same core observations, engineers can quickly spot missing retrieval, slow tools, model errors, and fallback branches.

cards.title: Trace Id Snippet
cards.prompt: Trace ids connect user reports, logs, datasets, and incident notes.
cards.explanation: A stable trace identifier lets teams move from a support ticket to the exact model and tool behavior behind it.

cards.title: Observation Snippet
cards.prompt: Name observations after product operations, not implementation trivia.
cards.explanation: Names like retrieve-policy and draft-answer remain understandable during incidents. Names like callHelper2 do not.

cards.title: Generation Metadata Snippet
cards.prompt: A generation should capture model identity and safe usage facts.
cards.explanation: Generation metadata helps compare model behavior, token usage, and latency across prompt versions and releases.

cards.title: Trace Anatomy
cards.prompt: What observations would you expect in a traced support-answer request?
cards.explanation: A strong answer includes classify intent, retrieve sources, optional tool call, model generation, output check, and final status.

cards.title: Tracing And Privacy
cards.prompt: How do you keep traces useful without turning them into a data leak?
cards.explanation: Capture stable ids, versions, source references, and outcome metadata. Redact or avoid secrets, credentials, unnecessary personal data, and raw private documents.

cards.title: Trace Versus Session
cards.prompt: When would you use a session instead of only a trace?
cards.explanation: Use sessions when a user journey spans multiple traces, such as a multi-turn conversation or task with several requests.

cards.title: Prompt Version
cards.prompt: A prompt version is a product behavior version, not just a text edit.
cards.explanation: Prompt changes can affect tone, policy compliance, latency, cost, refusal behavior, and citation quality, so they need review and evaluation.

cards.title: Dataset
cards.prompt: A dataset stores examples used to test prompt and model behavior.
cards.explanation: Datasets make experiments repeatable. They should include easy cases, edge cases, missing context, and examples from production failures.

cards.title: Scores
cards.prompt: Scores turn LLM outputs into reviewable quality signals.
cards.explanation: Scores can be boolean, categorical, numeric, or text. Use the simplest shape that supports the release decision.

cards.title: Keep A Baseline
cards.prompt: Run experiments against the current production behavior before declaring a prompt better.
cards.explanation: A new prompt is only better relative to a baseline and the scores the product actually cares about.

cards.title: Hard Cases Matter
cards.prompt: A dataset with only happy paths will approve fragile prompts.
cards.explanation: Include ambiguity, missing context, adversarial phrasing, policy limits, and known previous failures to catch realistic regressions.

cards.title: Human Review
cards.prompt: Use human annotations when correctness depends on policy or domain judgment.
cards.explanation: Automated judges are useful, but some quality dimensions need domain experts to build ground truth and calibrate later automation.

cards.title: Grounding Score Snippet
cards.prompt: A grounding score can start as deterministic citation checks.
cards.explanation: Simple code evaluators can catch obvious failures before more expensive model-based review is needed.

cards.title: Decision Rule Snippet
cards.prompt: Write the experiment decision rule before running the experiment.
cards.explanation: A predeclared rule reduces cherry-picking and helps stakeholders agree on what quality means.

cards.title: Dataset Item Snippet
cards.prompt: Dataset items should include expected behavior, not just input text.
cards.explanation: Expected behavior can be an answer, refusal, escalation, or required source. This makes evaluation match product intent.
cards.code: const item = { input, expected: { behavior: 'escalate', reason: 'missing source' } };

cards.title: Prompt Release
cards.prompt: How would you release a new production prompt safely?
cards.explanation: A strong answer includes versioning, trace linkage, dataset experiments, scoring, staged rollout, monitoring, and rollback.

cards.title: Score Design
cards.prompt: Why might one overall quality score be insufficient?
cards.explanation: Different risks need separate signals, such as groundedness, helpfulness, policy compliance, escalation correctness, latency, and cost.

cards.title: Dataset Source
cards.prompt: Why add production failure traces to evaluation datasets?
cards.explanation: Production failures reveal realistic cases that synthetic happy paths often miss. They turn incidents into regression coverage.

cards.title: RAG Quality Is System Quality
cards.prompt: RAG quality combines retrieval, context, prompts, output policy, and evaluation.
cards.explanation: A model cannot answer from trusted context if retrieval returns the wrong, stale, unauthorized, or excessive source material.

cards.title: Stale Source
cards.prompt: A stale source used to be correct but no longer represents current truth.
cards.explanation: Stale documents are dangerous because they produce plausible answers. Source versioning and freshness filters make this failure visible.

cards.title: Permission Filter
cards.prompt: RAG retrieval must respect what the user is allowed to see.
cards.explanation: A relevant source is not valid if the user lacks permission. Permission filters belong before prompt construction.

cards.title: Trace Source IDs
cards.prompt: Record source ids and versions for every RAG answer.
cards.explanation: Source ids let the team inspect whether retrieval, prompt context, citation behavior, or model generation caused a bad answer.

cards.title: Missing Context
cards.prompt: A good RAG assistant can say it does not have enough source context.
cards.explanation: Fallbacks are safer than unsupported answers. Missing-context cases should be represented in evaluation datasets.

cards.title: Citation Check
cards.prompt: A citation should support the claim it is attached to.
cards.explanation: Citation presence is not enough. Teams should review whether the cited source actually backs the generated answer.

cards.title: Citation Status Snippet
cards.prompt: Start citation checking by validating cited ids against retrieved ids.
cards.explanation: This does not prove semantic support, but it catches missing and unknown citations quickly.
cards.code:
const retrievedIds = new Set(sources.map((s) => s.id));
const unknown = answer.citedSourceIds.filter((id) => !retrievedIds.has(id));

cards.title: Context Budget Snippet
cards.prompt: Context budgets prevent retrieval from flooding the prompt.
cards.explanation: Token budgeting forces the retriever and prompt builder to prioritize the strongest evidence instead of dumping everything into context.

cards.title: Fallback Snippet
cards.prompt: Use explicit fallback status when sources are insufficient.
cards.explanation: Explicit status makes missing-context cases searchable in traces and reusable as evaluation examples.

cards.title: RAG Failure Modes
cards.prompt: Name three RAG failure modes and how you would observe them.
cards.explanation: Strong answers include no hit, wrong hit, stale source, permission leak, context overload, and citation mismatch with trace fields for each.

cards.title: RAG Dataset
cards.prompt: What cases belong in a serious RAG evaluation dataset?
cards.explanation: Include factual lookup, ambiguity, missing answer, stale policy, permission boundaries, multi-document synthesis, and adversarial retrieved text.

cards.title: RAG With Langfuse
cards.prompt: How does Langfuse help debug bad RAG answers?
cards.explanation: Langfuse traces connect the question, retrieval query, source ids, prompt context, generation, citations, fallback status, and scores.

cards.title: Dynamic Choice
cards.prompt: Use an agent when the model genuinely needs to choose steps or tools.
cards.explanation: If the workflow is known, a deterministic graph or chain is easier to test and operate. Agent flexibility has real risk and cost.

cards.title: LangGraph Durability
cards.prompt: LangGraph is for durable execution, streaming, persistence, and human-in-the-loop control.
cards.explanation: Graph state and checkpoints matter when workflows need to pause, resume, stream progress, or survive beyond a single request.

cards.title: Human Approval
cards.prompt: Human approval is a design control for high-impact tool actions.
cards.explanation: Approval is appropriate for money movement, external messages, sensitive access, destructive actions, and legal or policy commitments.

cards.title: Least Privilege Tools
cards.prompt: Give agents narrow tools instead of one powerful general-purpose tool.
cards.explanation: Narrow tools are easier to authorize, validate, rate limit, trace, and review. Broad tools make model mistakes more dangerous.

cards.title: Idempotency Review
cards.prompt: Write-capable tools need idempotency and retry rules before production.
cards.explanation: Agents may retry or resume. Without idempotency, one user request can accidentally create duplicate side effects.

cards.title: Trace The Approval
cards.prompt: Trace both the model proposal and the human approval decision.
cards.explanation: Auditability requires the planned action, validated arguments, approving actor, decision time, and final tool result.

cards.title: Permission Matrix Snippet
cards.prompt: A permission matrix keeps agent tool authority visible in code.
cards.explanation: Visible permission logic is testable. Hidden permission logic inside a prompt is not enough for production side effects.

cards.title: Tool Budget Snippet
cards.prompt: Tool-call budgets protect systems from runaway agent loops.
cards.explanation: Budgets make stopping conditions explicit and help contain cost, latency, and dependency pressure.

cards.title: Approval Interrupt Snippet
cards.prompt: Durable workflows can pause for human approval before continuing.
cards.explanation: Human-in-the-loop interrupts are useful when a model proposes a high-impact action that needs explicit review.
cards.code: const approval = interrupt({ action: 'issue_refund', amount, invoiceId });

cards.title: Agent Operations
cards.prompt: What operational controls does a production agent need?
cards.explanation: Strong answers include tool schemas, least privilege, approval gates, budgets, tracing, checkpoint rules, idempotency, and fallback behavior.

cards.title: Why LangGraph
cards.prompt: When would you reach for LangGraph instead of a simple LangChain agent?
cards.explanation: Use LangGraph when you need explicit state, checkpoints, streaming, resume, interrupts, human-in-the-loop, or complex workflow control.

cards.title: Approval Design
cards.prompt: What should a human approval screen show before an agent writes data?
cards.explanation: Show the user request, proposed action, tool name, validated arguments, expected side effect, risk, and cancel or rollback options.

cards.title: Prompt Injection
cards.prompt: Prompt injection happens when user or external text steers model behavior unexpectedly.
cards.explanation: Prompt injection can be direct or indirect. Retrieved content should be treated as data, not as trusted instructions.

cards.title: Sensitive Data
cards.prompt: LLM traces, datasets, prompts, and outputs can all become data exposure surfaces.
cards.explanation: Decide what to store, redact, hash, exclude, and retain before production. Trace usefulness does not justify unnecessary sensitive data capture.

cards.title: Excessive Agency
cards.prompt: An agent has excessive agency when it can do more than the product task requires.
cards.explanation: Least privilege applies to conversational systems too. Do not give summarizers write tools or support bots unrestricted financial actions.

cards.title: Layered Controls
cards.prompt: Prompt wording alone does not solve LLM security risk.
cards.explanation: Use separation of instructions and data, validation, least privilege, approval gates, tracing, evaluation, and incident response together.

cards.title: Incident Packet
cards.prompt: LLM incidents need prompt version, model, trace ids, source ids, tool calls, and rollback path.
cards.explanation: These facts let teams reconstruct what happened and decide whether the issue came from prompt, retrieval, model, tool, or policy behavior.

cards.title: Govern Map Measure Manage
cards.prompt: Use AI risk frameworks as practical operating loops, not paperwork.
cards.explanation: Govern ownership, map risks, measure behavior, and manage mitigations across the feature lifecycle. This aligns policy with engineering practice.

cards.title: Risk Classifier Snippet
cards.prompt: Risk classifiers should fail closed for sensitive data and write actions.
cards.explanation: Simple deterministic gates can prevent the model from turning uncertain or high-risk requests into immediate side effects.

cards.title: Injection Flag Snippet
cards.prompt: Flag external instructions found in retrieved content for review.
cards.explanation: External instructions are not automatically malicious, but they should not be allowed to override system instructions or tool policy.

cards.title: Retention Snippet
cards.prompt: Trace retention should be explicit and matched to incident needs.
cards.explanation: Retention policy balances debugging value, privacy risk, compliance expectations, and cost.

cards.title: Prompt Injection Review
cards.prompt: How do you mitigate prompt injection in a RAG application?
cards.explanation: Strong answers separate instructions from data, validate tool calls, limit authority, trace behavior, include adversarial evals, and fail closed when uncertain.

cards.title: AI Governance
cards.prompt: What does practical AI governance look like for an engineering team?
cards.explanation: It includes owners, source-of-truth prompts, change logs, eval datasets, trace controls, incident playbooks, risk reviews, and release gates.

cards.title: Trace Data Risk
cards.prompt: What data protection questions should be answered before enabling LLM tracing?
cards.explanation: Ask what is captured, who can access it, how it is redacted, how long it is retained, and whether datasets copy production content.
